transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2028-01-17
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~58 minutes
Recorded at: 2028-01-17T15:00:00-08:00
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Aisha (Lodestar Head of ML), Tom (Lodestar Platform), Nina (CTO), Samir (Product)
Shared links: https://redwood.app/cost-models/lodestar-token-econ.xlsx (cost model), https://redwood.app/console/playbook/lodestar (console playbook), Security pack: https://redwood.app/security/soc2-+/lodestar (SOC2/KMS summary)

Summary (auto): Maya opened with agenda; Diego took the lead on the Optimize console walkthrough and cost-sim spreadsheet. Conversation covered session affinity, prefix (KV) caching patterns, expected hit rates, batching size tradeoffs, and security concerns for Private/Dedicated options. Action items and follow ups recorded.

00:00 Maya: okay uh good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. this is Maya from Redwood, with Diego and Jordan. we wanted to run through a token economics focused workshop and walk through recommended session cache and batching configurations tailored to Lodestar's commerce workload.
00:18 Aisha: thanks, yeah appreciate it. we mainly care about two things: keep latency under 220ms p95 for customer-facing completions, and cut our per-transaction token cost at least 30% from current baseline.
00:30 Diego: great, that's the right target. quick question on current traffic shape — Tom, do you have rough numbers for median session length and how many concurrent users during peak?
00:42 Tom: yeah, peak concurrency is around 1.8k active sessions, median session length is about 18 turns, mean tokens per turn roughly 60 tokens. there is a long tail with a few sessions at thousands of tokens for complex dev chats.
00:58 Jordan: okay that distribution is helpful, thanks. we can prot a couple of strategies: short-term you get big wins with prefix/KV caching and lookahead; medium-term you use session-affinity + batching tuned to your tail; long-term dedicated pools with quantized models.
01:15 Nina: can you explain the prefix or kv cache again — like what exactly gets cached and how do you control expiry?
01:25 Diego: yeah so prefix cache targets the repeated prefix tokens we expect in a session — for commerce that might be user profile + product context + last-turn embeddings. Redwood's KV cache stores the key/value attention cache for prefixes and can be hit across requests if session affinity or a session-id key is used. TTLs are configurable per-route; typical pattern is 30min to 2 hours depending on session recency.
01:48 Aisha: and what's the hit rate we can realistically expect?
01:52 Diego: depends — with session affinity and sticky routing we often see 35-60% effective KV hit rate for returning sessions, higher for assistant-style bots. with aggressive lookahead/prefetch (we kick off the next chunk when user is idle) you can push effective savings further — maybe up to 70% in some workloads, but that assumes predictable next-turn behavior.
02:15 Tom: what are the latency implications of KV cache misses vs hits?
02:20 Diego: a cache hit returns much faster because the runtime can skip recomputing early layers and key/value recompute; hit latency delta is model/hardware-dependent but typically 20-120ms savings per request on our GPU runtime for large contexts. misses pay the full compute cost; we show this in the spreadsheet as tokens and ms per stage.
02:38 Maya: importantly from a cost perspective, hits are the unit savings — fewer effective tokens and less decode work. Jordan, can you jump into the cost model?
02:47 Jordan: sure. uploaded the Lodestar sheet — you can see three baseline scenarios: 1) no caching, batch size 1; 2) session-affinity with prefix cache TTL 45m, batch size 4; 3) prefetch + lookahead + batch size 8. the spreadsheet models GPU compute + egress + amortized infra.
03:08 Aisha: looking at scenario 2, it claims 38% token cost reduction. where is most of that coming from?
03:15 Jordan: mostly from prefix KV hits — that removes forward-pass compute for the cached prefix tokens and reduces average tokens per request. Batching helps by increasing hardware utilization, so per-token GPU cost goes down. the spreadsheet has a per-token composite cost line.
03:31 Tom: okay but batching increases latency at low QPS sometimes, right? how do you balance p95 latency with batch windows?
03:38 Diego: yes there's a tradeoff — we use dynamic batching with latency budgets. Redwood can cap batch delay to ensure your p95 stays under 220ms. for example you can set max batching delay 15ms and a max batch size of 8; this gives most of the batching efficiency while keeping latency bounded. at low QPS batching doesn't hurt because we fall back to immediate execution.
04:00 Nina: what about dedicated vs hosted — is Dedicated necessary to guarantee those p95 numbers at scale?
04:06 Maya: Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and consistent throughput, which makes latency predictable. Hosted can meet your SLOs too if you pick appropriate model variants and rely on our smart routing. but Dedicated removes noisy neighbor risks and simplifies audits for regulated payments flows.
04:22 Aisha: security question — for Private deployment can we use our KMS and HSM for key material?
04:28 Maya: yes, Redwood Private integrates with customer-managed KMS; HSM integrations are available for enterprise plans. we also provide audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and can run through SOC2 artifacts. we will share the security pack after this call.
04:44 Samir: what's the effort to enable prefix caching for our product routes? are there SDK changes?
04:50 Diego: minimal. you annotate routes with a session-id and decide which prefix to cache from your side. Redwood Console has a route-level toggle for prefix/KV cache and a simulator so you can estimate savings before enabling. we can also instrument custom hooks to warm the cache server-side.
05:05 Tom: you mentioned lookahead/prefetch — what is that exactly and does it waste compute if user abandons the flow?
05:12 Jordan: lookahead means we speculatively compute next tokens for expected next-turns. it can waste work on abandons, but the spreadsheet includes an abandon-rate param. if abandon-rate is low (users typically continue) you net savings because prefetching increases cache hit rate and lowers the cost per continued session. you can set conservative limits to reduce wasted compute.
05:33 Aisha: any examples of rule-of-thumb parameters you recommend for commerce chat?
05:37 Diego: for commerce we usually recommend TTL 30-60m, max batch size 6-8, batching delay cap 10-20ms, lookahead depth 32 tokens per prefetched request, and monitor hit-rate daily for tuning. those are safe starting points.
05:53 Tom: show me the console now — specifically the Optimize tab and the simulate widget.
06:00 Diego: sure, sharing screen... (screen share noises) okay, here's the console. top right is the Optimize sandbox where you can toggle KV cache on route and run a synthetic replay. I'm loading your replay with Tom's sample traffic (sanitized).
06:20 Diego: running sim... it will produce projected token-savings, p95 latency estimate, and effective GPU utilization. note the timeline for step 2 outlines where savings are coming from.
06:35 Diego: simulation result: scenario A (no cache) — avg token/sec cost X, p95 240ms. scenario B (prefix cache + batch 4) — projected token cost -34%, p95 210ms. scenario C (prefetch + batch 8) — projected token cost -46%, p95 225ms. these numbers assume a 20% lookahead success.
07:05 Aisha: 225ms p95 for scenario C is slightly above our 220ms requirement — can we tighten configs to drop p95 a bit while keeping savings?
07:12 Diego: yes reduce batch delay cap to 8ms and cap batch size at 6, that typically brings p95 down ~10-15ms but you lose 3-5% savings. it's a knobs tradeoff.
07:30 Nina: curious about long-tail sessions with 8k contexts — how does cache behave there?
07:36 Jordan: for very long contexts we split into windowed prefixes, keep most recent chunk hot in KV, and evict older windows. long context still benefits from KV if earlier prefixes are reused; otherwise cost is dominated by full recompute for the long initial context. quantized models and offloading large context to cheaper endpoints can help.
07:55 Samir: what's an example of expected monthly dollar savings if we move from baseline to scenario C for our traffic?
08:02 Jordan: using your submitted traffic and current cost per token, the sheet projects $38k/mo baseline down to $21k/mo in scenario C — about 45% savings. caveats: depends on lookahead success and hit rates; we stress-tested with conservative abandon rates.
08:25 Tom: those are big numbers; whats the setup time to pilot this?
08:28 Maya: pilot can be quick: 1) we enable route-level prefix caching on a subset of traffic, 2) run live sim+bench for 2 weeks, 3) review metrics and decide on Dedicated/Private. typical pilot 3-6 weeks to get meaningful numbers.
08:45 Aisha: for pilot, we need SOC2 docs and proof of KMS integration before we start any customer-facing data in Private.
08:52 Maya: yes we'll send SOC2 + KMS integration notes. note that Hosted is acceptable for non-sensitive data but for payment tokens and PII we recommend Private with customer-managed KMS.
09:05 Tom: any pitfalls you've seen customers run into when enabling prefix cache?
09:10 Diego: common pitfalls: 1) using a too-broad session key so unrelated sessions hit same cache, 2) low TTL causing churn and no effective hits, 3) not instrumenting user abandon rates which makes prefetch look worse than it is. we usually ship a short checklist and the console warns on risky configurations.
09:30 Aisha: do you have benchmarks for model variants — like fp16 vs int8 quantization impact with batch sizes 4-8?
09:38 Jordan: yes — quantization reduces cost per token but can increase latency slightly depending on kernel selection. the Optimize tab includes preset quant profiles; in our tests int8 with batch 8 gave ~1.7x throughput improvements and 15-25% token-cost reduction versus fp16 for the same accuracy envelope. we include accuracy regression monitoring in the evals.
09:59 Samir: competitors — do you see Anthropic or others offering similar caching approaches?
10:05 Maya: some offer application-level caching primitives but Redwood's KV cache is runtime integrated and designed for attention cache reuse across requests which yields much larger wins for LLM workloads. we'll include a short competitive note.
10:18 Nina: let's talk SLAs — if we go Dedicated what's the SLA for latency and availability?
10:24 Maya: Dedicated plans have commit-backed throughput and a 99.95% uptime SLA; latency SLOs are per-model with p95 targets documented in the SOW. we'll include draft SOW language in the follow-up.
10:36 Tom: ok, for the bench Diego will need more instrumentation — I'll export the histogram of session inter-arrival times and the session-id distribution.
10:44 Diego: perfect — that'll help set TTLs and lookahead heuristics.
10:48 Jordan: quick note on cost model sensitivity: the sheet has sliders for lookahead success, abandon rate, and cache hit-rate. small changes to hit-rate produce significant savings changes, so we want live metrics during pilot.
11:03 Aisha: are there any regulatory/data residency issues if we use Hosted?
11:07 Maya: Hosted can be regionally isolated; Redwood supports region controls and data residency options. for strict residency or air-gapped requirements, Private or on-prem is recommended.
11:18 Samir: one last technical: if we use session-affinity routing and rebalancing, how do you handle token KV movement across nodes?
11:25 Diego: we shard KV by session-id and maintain sticky routing; for rebalancing we asynchronously replicate hot KV entries. worst case an on-miss causes recompute but we also persist small warm snapshots to reduce rebuild time.
11:42 Aisha: ok that makes sense. can you summarize next steps?
11:45 Maya: sure — recap: we will send the tailored cost-model spreadsheet and the console playbook links (Maya), Lodestar to share traffic histograms (Tom), Redwood to run bench with prefetched KV scenario (Diego), Lodestar to confirm security checklist and which routes to pilot (Aisha/Nina). schedule pilot kickoff for week of Jan 29.
11:58 Nina: thanks everyone, this was very useful.
12:01 Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with action items.

End of transcript.
